newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - STADIUM BEARS WITNESS TO FALLEN HERO.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - STADIUM BEARS WITNESS TO FALLEN HERO.

text.p: AKASZTO, Hungary, Dec 1 - For sale: first division stadium, nearly new, one careful owner, situated in the middle of the Great Hungarian Plain, plenty of parking space. Apply: Hungarian tax office.
So ends the dream of one of modern Hungary's most colourful characters -- Jozsef Stadler, 45, post-communist capitalist extraordinaire, owner of Stadler FC.
Stadler is the last of a generation of "entrepreneurs" who had the wits -- and the contacts -- to cash in on the first flush of unregulated trading following the end of communism.
He did so well he not only bought a football team, he brought it to his home village and built a stadium round it.
Now the Hungarian tax authorities are claiming several million dollars in tax arrears on Stadler's boom years in the early 1990s and have demanded he sell the stadium.

"Nobody will take it on. I built it and I'm going to hold on to it," he told Reuters in the VIP lounge of the gleaming 20,000-seater which towers over empty fields on the edge of the village of Akaszto, population 3,000.
Under central planning, Stadler, once a shepherd boy, became the commercial manager of the Bacs-Kiskun county's main trading company, setting up deals with other cooperatives in Hungary.
He thus had a ready-made network of contacts when the last communist government allowed private companies to start up in the late 1980s.
Short and stocky, and with the rosy complexion of Father Christmas, Stadler looks back on the early years with pride.

"When the changes started I set up a limited company to trade food and liquor wholesale to 5,000 shops nationwide," he said. "When Romania had its revolution and (President Nicolae) Ceausescu fell we got in quickly with food, TVs and cosmetics."
By 1993 he was trading with all Hungary's eastern neighbours, including the newly independent Ukraine.

"For people who work with Russians and Ukrainians there are different rules from the rest of Europe," he said. "I can't say anything bad about them, but it's tougher, you need money to ensure safe delivery of goods and protection."
That is something Stadler learnt the hard way.
In 1993 his company exported $105 million worth of goods, generating one billion forints' ($6 million) profit. It also generated the attention of organised crime.
On January 16, 1994, a group of armed men intercepted him as he left his office and drove him 40 miles (65 km) to a derelict building next to a Soviet barracks.
Stadler agreed to hand over the forint equivalent of $1 million and was released the following morning.
"Somebody who worked for me and knew all the company details was also the director of the local customs office and got in touch with the Chechen mafia," Stadler recounts.
But Stadler's problems were only beginning. The Hungarian tax authorities were also taking an interest in his success.

"I was so seriously present on the Russian market I wanted to increase my output by 500 percent," he remembers. "I reported this to the Hungarian authorities and asked if I was allowed that much business".
He also asked for VAT refunds and export subsidies worth a total 1.5 billion forints ($10 million).

The tax office responded by declaring his claim for export subsidies fraudulent, opened proceedings to recover what they said was 500 million forints ($3 million) in unpaid VAT and in 1995 sent the police to search Stadler's home.
Stadler, who has since closed his business and had to sack his 300-strong workforce, was finally told to put his beloved stadium on the market.
"I'm clean and I'll prove it in court," he says defiantly.

Meanwhile the fortunes of Stadler FC reflect those of its owner. On a crisp autumn day in front of 400 people scattered around the vast arena, his team lost 2-1 to the bottom club in the league, Siofok.
But while the team stutters, adulation for the owner remains undimmed among the spectators.
Mother-of-two Erzsebet Domjan works as a steward and has seen every match since the club was promoted.
"He's a hero, they love him in the village," she said.

"Everybody's very sad about Stadler's problems and has sympathy for him," said another fan, heating engineer Lajos Szabo, who was one of hundreds who brought wheelbarrows of earth from their garden to help build the terraces.
"He made our village unique in the world and it doesn't matter where the cash came from, it gave us jobs and money."
As for the stadium, with a price tag of $6 million and monthly heating, electricity and phone bills of $15,000, Stadler does not expect a queue of buyers outside his door.
"I can only see a foreign investor coming in," he said. "We could always call the team something like Coca-Cola-Stadler." 302341 GMT nov 96
